glossary.heroHighlight: for the events and venues industry
glossary.heroSubtitle: Definitions of the concepts we use at Ronda Privé and that you'll hear across the sector.

compra-anticipada.definition: Sales method where the customer buys and pays for their order days or weeks before the event. On event day, activate your purchase and collect it without standing in line. Helps the organizer plan inventory in advance.

compra-y-retiro.definition: Method where the customer orders from their phone during the event and collects it at a point of sale once it's ready. Works as a digital queue: no need to physically wait in line.

entrega-en-asiento.definition: Method for events with identified seats (stadiums, suites, boxes, hospitality). The customer scans the QR at their location, orders from their phone, and receives the order directly at their seat or table — without moving.

fila-digital.definition: System that replaces the physical line with a digitally managed queue. The customer orders from their phone, receives an order number, and approaches the pickup point only when the order is ready.

numero-de-orden.definition: Unique identifier the customer receives at checkout. Used to collect the order, and depending on the organizer's setup, may be requested alongside an additional verification code.

punto-de-venta.definition: Physical space or digital system where a sale is completed. At events, traditional points of sale include bars, cash registers, and kiosks. A platform like Ronda Privé works as a digital POS without dedicated hardware.

totem-de-autoservicio.definition: Physical terminal located at the venue where the customer assembles and pays for their order. Requires infrastructure (screen, card reader, maintenance) and takes up space. It's the alternative replaced by mobile ordering.

carta-digital.definition: Product menu accessible from the customer's phone. Allows updating prices, adding promotions, and disabling out-of-stock products without printing physical menus.

inventario-tiempo-real.definition: Stock tracking that updates with each completed sale. Lets you see available inventory by product and by point of sale, detect stockouts before they happen, and restock with time to spare.

dashboard.definition: Interface for the event organizer that consolidates sales metrics, active orders, inventory, and operational configuration. Centralizes operations in a single view.

pwa.definition: App that runs in the phone's browser but behaves like a native app: fast loading, the ability to work offline for moments, can be added to the home screen. No download from an app store required.

qr.definition: Square image that encodes a link or data. The customer scans it with the phone's camera and opens the event menu or order directly. Replaces the need to download apps or type URLs.

modo-cache.definition: The platform's ability to keep operating during a temporary loss of internet connection. Actions are saved locally and synced as soon as signal returns.

trazabilidad.definition: Record of each order's state from purchase to delivery: received, in preparation, ready, delivered. Helps resolve disputes with customers and measure actual preparation times.

cloud.definition: External servers — in Ronda Privé's case, AWS — that process orders without the venue needing local hardware. Guarantees availability during demand peaks and eliminates the risk of failure from physical equipment.

venue.definition: Physical place where an event is held or where a hospitality business operates. Includes everything from stadiums and festivals to bars, restaurants, and coffee shops.

suite.definition: Private space within a stadium or arena, generally with hospitality service included. Features direct view of the event, dedicated furniture, and personalized attention.

palco.definition: Elevated, private section within a theater, stadium, or venue. Differs from general seating in privacy and service. Can be corporate or private.

hospitality.definition: Premium service within an event that includes food, drinks, and personalized attention. Usually sold as an add-on to general admission and operates with different dynamics than a mass bar.

festival.definition: Mass event, generally outdoors, with one or more musical stages and lasting one to several days. Characterized by high simultaneous attendance and multiple points of sale.

coffee-shop.definition: Hospitality establishment with constant customer flow but smaller scale than a mass event. Operates all day and handles a high turnover of small orders.

ticket-promedio.definition: Average monetary value of each transaction during an event. Calculated by dividing total revenue by transaction count. One of the main KPIs for evaluating point-of-sale performance.

tiempo-de-espera.definition: Minutes a customer spends between ordering and receiving their order. At mass events, can reach 15-30 minutes at a physical bar; with mobile ordering, typically drops to 2-3 minutes.

rotacion-de-barra.definition: Number of customers a point of sale can serve per hour. High turnover means more sales in the same physical space. Key indicator for sizing an event's operation.

tasa-de-conversion.definition: Percentage of event attendees who actually purchased consumption. Low conversion indicates potential attendees didn't get to buy — usually due to long lines or stockouts.

post1.title: How to increase F&B sales at large-scale events
post1.excerpt: Proven strategies to maximize per-attendee spending and capture revenue lost in queues.
post1.intro: At a large-scale event, food and beverage sales can account for a major share of total revenue. Yet much of that revenue is lost to an avoidable cause: friction. Long queues, saturated points of sale, and attendees who would rather not miss the show than wait for a drink.

sections.heading: The invisible cost of queues
sections.body:
Once the line stretches past a few minutes, part of the crowd simply gives up. That sale is not recovered: consumption at events is impulse-driven and tied to the moment. If the impulse passes, the purchase never happens.

Demand is not evenly spread either — it concentrates in peaks: halftime, artist changeovers, the minutes before the headliner. That is exactly when service capacity collapses and the most sales are lost.

sections.heading: Turning every location into a point of sale
sections.body:
The most direct way to sell more is not opening more bars but multiplying purchase points without extra infrastructure. With mobile ordering via QR, every seat, table, or section becomes a point of sale.

Attendees order from where they are and pick up when the order is ready, or receive it right at their seat. The bar stops being the only channel and demand spreads out.

sections.heading: Capturing demand before the event
sections.body:
Pre-event ordering captures revenue days or weeks in advance: attendees pay upfront and simply show their QR code to pick up on event day.

For organizers that means earlier cash flow, known demand, and less congestion at the moments of highest operational pressure.

sections.heading: Measuring in real time to react in time
sections.body: Without live data, problems surface only after they have already cost sales. A dashboard with real-time sales and inventory lets you shift staff toward high-demand points, restock before running out, and adjust the operation during the event — not after it.

post2.title: The future of F&B technology at events
post2.excerpt: Global trends in digitizing food and beverage sales across the events industry.
post2.intro: Food and beverage sales at events are changing fast. What used to be cash and a register a few years ago is now digital payment, QR ordering, and real-time data. These are the trends setting the industry's direction.

sections.heading: From cash to digital payments
sections.body: Digital payment has gone from differentiator to baseline expectation. Across the region, adoption of digital wallets and contactless payments keeps growing, and events follow the same curve: less cash in circulation means faster operations, fewer register errors, and full traceability of every sale.

sections.heading: Web apps instead of downloads
sections.body:
Native apps have a structural problem at events: nobody wants to download an app to buy a drink. PWAs (progressive web apps) remove that friction — attendees scan a QR code and buy instantly from the browser, with no downloads or lengthy sign-ups.

For organizers, that translates into adoption rates far higher than any app that requires installation.

sections.heading: Consumption data as an asset
sections.body:
Every digital order generates information: what sells, at what time, in which section, and at what price. That history lets you plan upcoming events on real demand instead of intuition: how much stock to load, where to place points of sale, and which products to push.

Organizers who accumulate this data event after event make decisions their competitors are still guessing at.

sections.heading: Toward a frictionless operation
sections.body: The direction is clear: fewer queues, less hardware, more integration. Pre-event ordering connected to ticketing, in-seat delivery, and inventory synced across points of sale all point the same way — buying inside an event should be as simple as buying from any online store.

post3.title: How to reduce queues in stadiums: a case study
post3.excerpt: Analysis of how digital ordering implementation reduced wait times by 70% at a stadium.
post3.intro: Stadiums concentrate one of the toughest operational challenges in F&B: tens of thousands of people trying to buy within the same window of minutes. This analysis walks through what happens when digital ordering is deployed by section, and what results to expect.

sections.heading: The starting point
sections.body: The pattern repeats across most stadiums: sales concentrate at halftime and show breaks. In those minutes, queues outgrow service capacity, a large share of the crowd gives up, and per-attendee sales stay far below their potential.

sections.heading: What was implemented
sections.body:
The rollout combined two modes: in-seat ordering for premium sections — attendees scan the QR at their location and get the order delivered where they sit — and order-and-pickup for the rest of the venue, with pickup points split by section to spread the flow of people.

No additional infrastructure was installed: the operation runs on existing points of sale and attendees' own phones.

sections.heading: The results
sections.body:
With digital ordering live, wait times dropped by around 70%: orders are prepared while attendees remain in their seats, and pickup takes seconds instead of minutes in line.

The commercial effect follows: with the waiting barrier removed, more attendees buy and order frequency rises throughout the event.

sections.heading: Lessons for other rollouts
sections.body: Three factors made the difference: clear signage so the crowd understands the pickup flow, brief staff training on the new preparation flow, and a focused menu that keeps preparation times stable even at peak demand.

post4.title: Real-time inventory management for events
post4.excerpt: Best practices for stock control, avoiding stockouts, and optimizing operations during an event.
post4.intro: At an event there is no 'restock tomorrow': stock that runs out during the show is lost revenue that never comes back. That is why inventory management at events has rules of its own — and real-time visibility is the first one.

sections.heading: Why inventory breaks at events
sections.body:
An event compresses a week's worth of normal demand into a few hours. With spreadsheets or manual counts, organizers find out about a stockout when the product is already gone — and every minute without stock at a high-demand point is revenue evaporating.

The opposite problem is costly too: overstock ends up as waste or immobilized capital.

sections.heading: Live visibility per point of sale
sections.body: Real-time inventory shows what remains of each product at every bar or point of sale, updated with each order. That turns stock into a variable you manage during the event: if one bar runs out of a product, it gets redistributed from another before sales are lost.

sections.heading: Alerts and decisions during the show
sections.body: Alert thresholds let you act before the stockout: when a product drops below a set level, the team knows instantly. Decisions stop depending on someone 'noticing' — the system alerts, the team executes.

sections.heading: What remains after the event
sections.body: At closing, the data tells the full story: what sold, at what pace, where stockouts happened, and how much waste remained. On that basis, the next event is planned on real demand: tighter purchasing, better distribution across points of sale, and less immobilized capital.

post5.title: Innovation in nightclubs: the new era of digital sales
post5.excerpt: How the most exclusive nightclubs are transforming the purchase experience with mobile technology.
post5.intro: In a nightclub, the experience is the product. And few things damage the experience more than spending twenty minutes trying to order a drink at a saturated bar. The most exclusive clubs understood this and are redesigning sales around mobile technology.

sections.heading: The bar as a bottleneck
sections.body: The bar concentrates the club's entire sales into a few meters: at peak hours, waits grow, guests get frustrated, and they consume less. Every minute in line is a minute off the dance floor — and a round that may never get ordered.

sections.heading: Tables and VIP: service without interruptions
sections.body:
A QR per table changes the service dynamic: the group orders from their phones and the order arrives at the table, without anyone walking to the bar or flagging down a waiter.

In VIP areas the effect is stronger: service feels premium precisely because it demands no effort, and the table keeps its consumption active all night.

sections.heading: Turnover and average ticket
sections.body: Less waiting translates directly into more rounds per night. When ordering takes seconds, consumption frequency rises and the average ticket per table grows — no sales pressure, just removing the friction that used to hold purchases back.

sections.heading: What to look for when choosing technology for a club
sections.body: Three practical criteria: it should require no additional hardware or app downloads, it should run reliably in a club's real conditions — low light, dense crowds, unstable signal — and it should deliver data per table and per product so you can manage the business, not just charge.

post6.title: Pre-event ordering: the strategy that maximizes revenue
post6.excerpt: Why pre-event sales are the most powerful tool for increasing predictability and revenue.
post6.intro: Of the three digital sales modes at events, pre-event ordering has the greatest impact on business predictability: it turns future demand into present revenue and into information for planning.

sections.heading: What it is and how it works
sections.body: Pre-event ordering lets attendees buy their consumption days or weeks before the event, right alongside the decision to attend. On event day, they simply show their QR code and pick up — no lines, no payments at the venue.

sections.heading: Revenue before doors open
sections.body: The financial effect is immediate: part of the event's sales comes in ahead of time, improving cash flow and reducing dependence on how the night goes. For events with high production costs, that advance can fund part of the operation.

sections.heading: Planning on real demand
sections.body: Every pre-event purchase is a confirmed demand data point: how many people will consume, which products, and in what volume. With that information, stock and staffing are sized on real demand instead of estimates — fewer stockouts, less waste, and a tighter operation.

sections.heading: How to communicate it so it works
sections.body: Pre-event ordering performs when it is built into the event's communication: offer it at the moment of ticket purchase, remind attendees in the days before, and attach a concrete incentive — convenience, perks, or preferred pickup access. The more natural the step from 'I have my ticket' to 'I have my first round,' the better it works.
